Past.text: Heritage was community-owned, tied to rituals, daily life, and local identity → people protected it naturally.
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: Intangible Heritage: Preservation wasn't about a static building but about passing down intangible heritage like oral stories, songs, and traditional crafts. Collective Ownership: Heritage sites, like temples or public squares, were collectively owned and managed by the community. They were places of daily use, not just monuments to be viewed. Local Identity: Heritage was inextricably linked to local identity and social cohesion. A village's history was its own, and protecting it was a matter of pride and continuity.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Many heritage sites are “museum- ified,” separated from communities → younger generations feel detached.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Present.text: Heritage is often detached from daily life. Museum-ification: Many heritage sites have become static "museums "for tourists, leading to a separation from the communities they originated from. Youth Disconnect: Younger generations, exposed to global culture, often feel detached and apathetic towards their local heritage, which can seem irrelevant.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Future.text: Heritage becomes living and participatory again, with co-creation (festivals, AR/VR engagement, inclusive access for all).
Future.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: Co-creation: Heritage will be participatory again, with communities actively co-creating festivals, art, and events. Inclusive Access: Technology like AR and VR will make heritage accessible to everyone, regardless of location or physical ability, fostering inclusive access for all.
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Past.text: Weak or colonial-era heritage laws, often focused on “monuments” not living culture.
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: Politics focused on state ownership and nationalism. State-Driven Protection: Heritage was primarily a tool for nationalism and state identity, with governments controlling preservation effor ts. Reactive Laws: Laws were often created in response to specific threats, like looting during war, rather than as a proactive, comprehensive strategy.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Politics is now more complex and collaborative. Soft Power: Heritage is used as a tool for "soft power, "promoting a country's culture and influence on the global stage. International Cooperation: There's a greater emphasis on international agreements and organi zations like UNESCO to protect heritage, though political disputes can still hamper these effor ts.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: UNESCO designations, national laws, and heritage bodies exist → but often siloed, underfunded, or mismanaged.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: Politics will integrate heritage into global issues. Global Security: Heritage will become a matter of global security and peacebuilding, with legal and political frameworks to prevent destruction in conflict zones. Climate Policy: Heritage protection will be a core component of climate policy, with governments creating legislation to protect sites from environmental threats.
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Future.text: Dynamic, digital-first governance of heritage → global databases, community-driven policy input, stronger enforcement with transparency.
Future.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: Heritage sustained by local economies (crafts, festivals, pilgrimages).
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: Funding was primarily a cost, with limited revenue streams. Preservation was seen as a financial burden, funded mainly by public funds and philanthropy rather than as a source of income.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Heritage is now an economic asset. The focus is on sustainable tourism and public-private partnerships to generate revenue for conservation and create jobs in local communities.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Tourism drives revenue but also over- commerciali z es heritage; many sites underfunded.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: Heritage will be a catalyst for new economies. Innovative models like blockchain for ethical provenance and heritage-led urban regeneration will create new value and ensure long-term sustainability.
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Future.text: Circular heritage economies → blending tourism, craft markets, local food, and sustainable models that fund preservation without exploitation.
Future.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: There was little to no competition for cultural heritage. It was seen as an intrinsic part of a community's identity, with its value being spiritual and historical, not commercial.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Past.text: Culture seen as identity, continuity, and pride, not competition.
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Present.text: Competition is primarily for city branding and tourism. Cities use their heritage to stand out, often in a superficial way, attracting visitors with a focus on revenue over preservation. This can lead to the commodification of culture.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Cities use heritage for branding (e.g., “Heritage Cities,” cultural tourism) → but often superficial.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: The competition will be about authenticity and sustainability. Cities will differentiate themselves by showing how well they preserve their heritage and integrate it into a modern, thriving community, making it a key part of their sustainable tourism strategy and global reputation.
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Future.text: Heritage becomes a differentiator for sustainable tourism and global recognition → cities “compete” by showing how well they preserve and integrate heritage into modern life.
Future.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: Heritage preserved only through physical monuments and oral traditions.
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: Technology was a passive tool for simple documentation. M ethods included basic photography, hand-drawn sketches, and written records. The primary goal was creating a physical archive for research and reference, not for public engagement.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Technology is a critical tool for both preservation and engagement. 3D scanning and photogrammetry create precise digital twins of sites and artifacts. Drones and remote sensing are used for large-scale, remote monitoring to detect threats in real- time.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Digital archiving, 3D scanning, AR/VR museums → still fragmented, mostly top-down.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: Immersive heritage ecosystems → digital twins of monuments, interactive storytelling, global open-source heritage databases accessible to all.
Future.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: Technology will be preventative, immersive, and decentraliz ed. AI will be used for predictive analysis to anticipate and prevent damage to sites before it occurs. AR and VR will create fully immersive and interactive experiences, allowing people to explore and learn about heritage in new ways
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Past.text: • Heritage laws often colonial in origin, focused only on monumental structures. • Weak enforcement, poor documentation, and little community input.
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: Regulations were reactive and limited. Laws were often created to address a specific crisis, like war-time looting, and were not comprehensive. They focused on individual, tangible obj ects rather than the broader cultural context or site protection.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: There's a push for global, complex frameworks. International conventions like the 1970 UNESCO Convention target illicit trafficking. National laws are becoming stricter, but enforcement often struggles to keep up with the speed and scale of illegal activities.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: • UNESCO conventions, national heritage laws, heritage city missions exist. • Gaps: underfunded bodies, corruption, fragmented policies, slow legal action.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: • Dynamic regulatory systems with real-time monitoring (AI, IoT, satellite). • Laws expand to cover intangible heritage (oral traditions, festivals, crafts). • Participatory governance → community, NGOs, and government co-regulating heritage.
Future.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: Regulations will be proactive, integrated, and technology-driven. New laws will explicitly address emerging threats like climate change and digital trafficking. Regulations will mandate the use of technologies like blockchain for provenance tracking and AI for monitoring.
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Past.text: Environmental threats to heritage rarely considered.
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Past.text: The concept was nationalist and selective. Only a few "masterpieces "or ancient wonders were considered important enough for protection. The idea of "universal "was limited and often defined by Western standards.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: Climate change, pollution, and urban expansion severely threaten monuments and natural heritage.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Present.text: The concept of Outstanding Universal Value is central. It holds that certain sites are so significant they transcend national boundaries and are part of the common heritage of all humanity, as defined by the UNESCO W orld Heritage Convention.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Future.text: Heritage embedded into climate resilience and urban planning, with universal frameworks (UNESCO + SDG integration) protecting both tangible and intangible heritage.
Future.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: The focus will be on the universality of threats. Climate change, armed conflict, and pollution are global problems that req uire a unified, universal response to protect our shared heritage for future generations.
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Past.text: The market was unregulated and opa que. Looting and illegal excavation fueled an underground market. There was a lack of provenance tracking, and stolen artifacts were easily sold to private collectors.
Past.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Past.text: • Heritage sustained by traditional markets (local crafts, pilgrimages, cultural festivals). • Economic value tied to daily life, not formaliz ed.
Past.author: Kanika Khosla

Present.text: The market is now a complex ecosystem. A growing, legitimate market for heritage tourism and related goods coexists with a sophisticated black market. Online platforms have made the illegal trade faster and more difficult to track.
Present.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Present.text: • Tourism is the main heritage market driver, often leading to over- commerciali zation. • Craftspeople/artisans struggle due to industrial substitutes and global competition.
Present.author: Kanika Khosla

Future.text: The market will be defined by ethical transparency. Technologies like blockchain will create a verifiable, public chain of custody for artifacts. This will make it harder for illegal goods to enter the legitimate market and will build trust for buyers and sellers.
Future.author: Sonia Wadhwani

Future.text: • Circular heritage markets → sustainable tourism, heritage-based creative industries, local supply chains. • Technology-enabled marketplaces (digital craft platforms, virtual cultural tourism). • Heritage as a competitive economic advantage (cities branded by authentic cultural economies).
Future.author: Kanika Khosla
